documents.abstract: Observation is a fundamental scientific practice in science learning, particularly for understanding gradual biological phenomena such as plant adaptation. Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, limited research has examined how AI-supported tools influence students' observation practices during authentic scientific inquiry. This study investigates the emergence and development of students' observation practices during plant adaptation learning supported by an AI-based identifier. A six-week mixed-methods exploratory study was conducted with 84 middle school students. Learning activities were organised into four phases: orientation, initial observation, AI-assisted identification, and re-observation and validation. Data were collected through observation sheets, students' observation notes, reflective journals, group discussions, and records of AI use. Quantitative analysis revealed significant differences in observation orientations across learning phases (Friedman test, p < .001), indicating changes in observation practices over time. Qualitative findings showed that students initially relied on AI-generated cues to guide their observations. Over time, however, observation practices shifted toward direct empirical observation and peer-supported validation through repeated comparisons of plant characteristics across environmental conditions. The findings reveal a developmental trajectory from AI-reliant observation to direct observation and collaborative validation, accompanied by a gradual reduction in dependence on AI-generated outputs. These findings suggest that AI may function as an initial observational scaffold, while more sophisticated observation practices emerge through repeated engagement with phenomena and collaborative reasoning.

We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This systematic review analyzed 46 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, revealing eight digital technology types, including Information and Communication Technology, Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Open Educational Resources, Massive Open Online Courses, Learning Management System, and Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality. Design/Approach/Method Technologies are organized across three conceptual layers: Infrastructure, Algorithm, and Application Layer. This study aims to investigate: (a) the key functions and implementation barriers of eight emerging technology types; (b) their impacts on teachers’ autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and (c) their impacts on the equity, quality, and efficiency of scalable teacher professional development. Findings Findings reveal that all technologies demonstrate dual impacts on the three psychological needs, both enabling and constraining, with competence most consistently supported across layers. Equity outcomes prove most challenging. Originality/Value This review concludes that effective technology integration requires human-centered ecosystems that amplify, not replace, teacher agency, advancing a value-rational approach recognizing teachers’ professional flourishing as an intrinsic good rather than an instrumental means.

Purpose This study systematically examines the intersection of emotional intelligence (EI), leadership and learning-oriented development to understand how the field has evolved and its implications for human resource development (HRD) theory and practice. Design/methodology/approach A bibliometric analysis of 72 Scopus-indexed, ABDC-ranked journal articles published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer. The analysis examined publication trends, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence patterns and thematic evolution within the field. Findings Seven thematic clusters emerged, with EI functioning as a central construct linking leadership, workplace learning and organizational outcomes. The findings indicate a shift from viewing EI as a fixed trait to conceptualizing it as a developable capability shaped through learning, reflection and relational experiences. The field has evolved from early conceptual exploration (2015–2018) to more empirical and context-driven research, particularly in the postpandemic period (2022–2025). While transformational leadership and EI remain dominant themes, adaptive, digital and crisis leadership have emerged as important areas of inquiry. The analysis also reveals a geographically diverse research landscape, although international collaboration remains uneven across regions. Originality/value This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the intersection between EI, leadership and learning and advances a learning-oriented perspective by positioning EI as a key capability within leadership development frameworks. By integrating leadership, workplace learning and organizational context, the study contributes to HRD and leadership scholarship and offers a structured foundation for future research and practice.

Purpose This study aims to examine the trends, intellectual structure, frequently explored topics, and future research directions in employee engagement within small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), thereby providing insights for theoretical development and HRM practice. Design/methodology/approach This review applied bibliometric methods to examine 730 documents indexed in the Scopus database and published between 1989 and 2024. The study utilized descriptive analyses and science mapping techniques, including co-citation and keyword co-occurrence analyses. Findings The findings reveal growing academic interest, highlighting a shift from transactional to transformational human resource management. Further research in South America and Africa is needed to improve the generalizability of the existing knowledge base. Three main clusters were identified along with influential authors and key theories in each area: “Integrated Psychological and Occupational Health”, “Dynamic Organizational Studies”, and “Work Engagement and Burnout”. Temporal co-word analysis shows the enduring relevance of job satisfaction and organizational commitment, with an emerging focus on the impacts of COVID-19 and sustainability, including corporate social responsibility (CSR), reflecting a trend toward integrating sustainable practices into business strategies. Originality/value To the authors' knowledge, this is the first bibliometric review focused specifically on employee engagement in the SME context, an important HRM issue for the effective management of human resources.

El presente trabajo muestra las tendencias administrativas contemporáneas como estrategias innovadoras aplicadas a las organizaciones, especialmente, el Empowerment que ayuda a reforzar el liderazgo y a incentivar la participación activa de los colaboradores en el sistema de gestión del riesgo la seguridad y salud en el trabajo (SG-SST). A partir de la revisión de la norma internacional ISO 45001 de 2018 y el Decreto 1072 de 2015 se logra evidenciar una problemática relacionada en la baja participación del capital humano en el tema de la prevención y la identificación de riesgos laborales. En este sentido, esta tendencia se propone como solución y estrategia para potencializar la participación activa de los colaboradores, incentivar la cultura del autocuidado en todas las áreas de la compañía. Lo cual contribuye a tener líderes íntegros, proporciona acciones preventivas más efectivas y eleva la comunicación interna. Por lo tanto, se verifica avances en el SG-SST enfocado en el liderazgo, en la asignación de responsabilidades, en la motivación de la participación activa de los colaboradores y la utilización de los diferentes recursos, integrando esta tendencia administrativa que permite mejorar de manera continua todo el proceso organizacional haciendo compañías más productivas, fortaleciendo la cultura de prevención de riesgos, accidentes e incidentes laborales.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
keywords: occupational health and safety management system

documents.abstract: Using adaptive intelligence as a theoretical lens, the study investigates how L2 motivational selves are associated with AI-IDLE engagement through psychological capital (PsyCap) and L2 grit and whether these indirect associations vary with AI literacy among 1025 Chinese university EFL learners. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM). For the ideal L2 self, associations with engagement emerged both directly and indirectly through PsyCap and L2 grit, whereas the ought-to L2 self showed an indirect association through PsyCap and no direct association with engagement. Higher AI literacy corresponded to stronger associations of both PsyCap and L2 grit with engagement. The two motivational self-guides were therefore associated with engagement through different psychological pathways, with AI literacy related to variation in the strength of these pathways. From an adaptive intelligence perspective, this conditional pattern indicates that the relevance of PsyCap and L2 grit to AI-IDLE engagement varies with learners’ AI literacy. These findings extend the application of adaptive intelligence to informal human–AI learning.

Modern English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pronunciation instruction has shifted its primary goal from native-like accent imitation to functional intelligibility and comprehensibility. Despite this paradigm shift, traditional classroom settings often struggle to provide personalized, real-time diagnostic feedback due to large class sizes and time constraints. This study investigates the pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven speech analysis and automated acoustic feedback in EFL pronunciation teaching. Synthesizing contemporary literature on Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) and feedback literacy, this paper examines how AI feedback impacts learner autonomy, segmental clarity, and suprasegmental awareness. The review reveals that AI tools provide consistent, low-anxiety practice environments that facilitate cognitive noticing and self-correction. However, over-reliance on automated metrics without explicit pedagogical framing can result in mechanical practice detached from communicative contexts. To reconcile these dynamics, this article introduces a conceptual Scaffolded Pedagogical Feedback Model (SPFM) that integrates AI-generated acoustic diagnostic data, structured peer dialogue, and teacher-mediated instructional intervention. The framework highlights the necessity of developing student feedback literacy to transform automated output into actionable learning strategies. Keywords: EFL pronunciation instruction, Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT), artificial intelligence, intelligibility, learner autonomy, feedback literacy.

This community service activity aimed to improve the understanding of senior high school and vocational high school students regarding classroom chair design based on anthropometric principles. The activity was conducted face-to-face at partner schools in Jakarta through ergonomics lectures, demonstrations of seated anthropometric measurements, percentile calculation exercises, and discussions on applying measurement results to chair dimensions. The anthropometric dimensions introduced included popliteal height, buttock-popliteal length, hip breadth, sitting shoulder height, and sitting elbow height. Evaluation was conducted through pre-tests and post-tests, question-and-answer sessions, observation of practical activities, analysis, and reflection. The results showed an improvement in participants’ understanding of anthropometric dimensions relevant to chair design. The proportion of participants who provided fully correct answers increased from 42.0% in the pre-test to 83.3% in the post-test. Participants were also able to identify the relationship between body dimensions and chair components, explain the risks associated with dimensional mismatch, and formulate initial principles for determining seat height, seat depth, seat width, and backrest dimensions. The activity demonstrated that contextual, practice-based learning can enhance students’ ergonomic literacy and encourage data-based thinking in evaluating learning facilities.

The rapid integration of generative AI tools has transformed writing instruction, raising questions about authorship, agency, and academic integrity in teacher education. Unlike search engines, generative AI produces synthesized text that supports brainstorming, drafting, revising, and feedback. While these tools can reduce cognitive load and enhance higher-order thinking, they may also weaken productive struggle, writer identity, and promote overreliance without intentional instructional design. These issues are especially relevant for preservice teachers who must learn to use AI both ethically and instructionally. Grounded in self-regulation, self-efficacy, metacognitive theory, and the cognitive process model of writing, this study frames AI as metacognitive scaffolding for writing development. The framework highlights a gap between preservice teachers' frequent use of AI and their limited readiness to teach with it. The article argues that intentional, theory-driven integration can support planning, monitoring, and reflection while preserving student voice and autonomy. I

Digital tools for eating-disorder support often rely on retrospective self-report or text-based prompts, offering limited support for the embodied, temporally unfolding nature of eating episodes. We introduce Embodied Therapeutic Interaction (ETI), a design framework for translating CBT-informed principles into phase-aligned, behavior-aware interactions, and instantiate it in EnjoyEAT, a prototype combining surface electromyography sensing with pre-meal preparation, in-meal awareness cues, and post-meal reflection. Formative inquiry with experts and people with lived experience yielded requirements concerning temporal vulnerability, bodily awareness, emotional safety, and autonomy-preserving feedback. A four-week, uncontrolled in-the-wild study with 12 participants reporting subclinical tendencies showed decreased EDE-Q scores and positive user-experience ratings. Interviews indicated feedback helped some participants notice and reflect on eating patterns, while revealing tensions around sensing accuracy, setup burden, and sustained engagement. Though not a clinical intervention, EnjoyEAT offers HCI design evidence about phase alignment, soft embodiment, reflective mediation, and emotionally careful feedback for situated recovery support.

This working paper examines whether the classical methodology of ʿilal al-Ḥadīth—the detection of hidden defects in apparently sound reports—can provide a useful conceptual framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence outputs in specialist knowledge environments. It develops the concept of the “epistemic hidden defect”: a weakness in provenance, attribution, inference, context, evidential hierarchy, or scholarly status that may remain concealed beneath a fluent and apparently authoritative AI-generated response. Drawing on classical Hadith-critical methodology and contemporary AI research, the paper distinguishes computational capability from scholarly authority. It develops the concepts of the Authority Ceiling, Digital Isnād, competence-specific human oversight, and the No-Autonomous-Grading Principle as safeguards for AI-assisted scholarship. The paper argues for an AI-assisted rather than AI-autonomous model of specialist research, in which computational systems widen the evidential field while consequential scholarly judgement remains traceable, reviewable, and accountable.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how generative AI disrupts the epistemic foundations of take-home academic assignments. It argues that written products can no longer be reliably interpreted as evidence of student thinking, as AI enables the production of fluent, academically credible work without corresponding cognitive effort. Drawing on teaching practice, the chapter shows how student submissions have shifted in form, tone, and ownership. It then reframes the problem as one of construct validity, where the link between performance and learning becomes unstable. In response, the chapter proposes presence-based assessment as a partial solution and argues that meaningful change requires institutional redesign of assessment architecture.

Following the introduction of publicly accessible AI and LLMs, they have gradually started to be adopted in the ESL classroom. Recent studies have revealed that these tools have had a wider impact on ESL assessment, allowing for enhanced accuracy, efficiency, and person alization in language evaluation. However, how widely these technologies are understood and used by teachers is still being investigated. This study explores how Serbian ESL teachers use and perceive ChatGPT as a tool for assessing student work. The study employs a mixed-methods approach, combining survey data from 53 participants with follow-up interviews from 10 educa tors to examine their tendencies, habits, and opinions regarding ChatGPT for assessment. Find ings revealed that grammar and vocabulary are the language skills which Serbian ESL teachers assessed most often using ChatGPT, while skills such as speaking, listening, and critical thinking were rarely assessed using AI. Teachers also expressed moderate trust in the tool’s ability to detect grammar and syntax errors, but were concerned about its limitations. These limitations included ChatGPT’s ability to provide accurate assessment, its tendency to give vague feedback, and its lack of contextual understanding. While many teachers recognized its ability to save time for as sessment tasks, they also recognized their own limited experiences with AI tools and stressed the need for human oversight, formal training, and ethical safeguards. This study indicated that even though ChatGPT does not yet have widespread use in the Serbian ESL classroom, interviewees frequently emphasized that it should be used as a supplementary tool to assist teachers, but that guidelines and professional training on its use need to be provided to the teachers before they would readily implement it in the classroom.

Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.

The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into marketing activities has transformed the way organizations interact with customers, analyze consumer behavior, and deliver personalized services. Despite the significant opportunities provided by AI technologies, their widespread adoption has also raised critical concerns regarding ethical risks, data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and customer trust. This chapter explores the role of responsible AI practices in mitigating marketing-related risks and enhancing customer confidence in AI-driven marketing environments. The chapter adopts a conceptual and analytical approach to examine the principles of ethical AI governance in marketing organizations, focusing on transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy protection, and human oversight. It further discusses how responsible AI practices contribute to reducing reputational risks, improving organizational credibility, and strengthening long-term customer relationships.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the ethical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education, emphasizing the need to align technological advancement with human agency, equity and sustainable innovation. It explores how AI is reshaping instructional practices, assessment systems, and educational governance across global and African contexts. Drawing on framework s such as UNESCO's recommendations on AI ethics and the OECD principles, this chapter per the authors analyses critical issues including algorithmic bias, overdependence, and the erosion of creativity. It further highlights the central role of teachers as ethical stewards, mediators, and facilitators of responsible AI use. The discussion underscores the importance of inclusive and assistive AI technologies in expanding access for marginalised learners while cautioning against reinforcing existing inequalities. Additionally, the chapter addresses policy, governance and accountability mechanisms necessary for ethical AI development advocating a human-centered approach that ensures AI supports educational goals.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) requires human involvement at every stage of its process. This paper proposes a systematic LLM evaluation protocol for end-to-end MCDA pipelines, using published expert rankings as a benchmark. In addition, it implements a four-stage LLM pipeline as a case study applying the protocol to three leading LLMs across five benchmark problems selected to vary in application domain and in the number of alternatives. The protocol comprises 225 independent pipeline executions (3 models × 5 repetitions × 3 temperatures × 5 problems); each execution applies three MCDA methods (LLM-weighted linear scoring, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE II) to the same LLM-generated score matrix, yielding 675 method-specific outputs in total. Consistent with a smaller pilot study of this protocol, differences between models are small relative to problem identity (Kruskal–Wallis, H = 1.10, p = 0.577, η2 = 0.005; a small but significant effect emerges once problem identity is controlled for, η2 = 0.6%), while problem identity remains the dominant performance factor—and a larger one than previously observed (η2 = 0.761, H = 170.51, p < 0.001, N = 225 executions). Kendall’s τ ranges from −0.34 on a ten-alternative problem to 0.56 on a four-alternative problem; a permutation test against random rankings indicates that two of the five benchmark problems produced agreement below chance level, while two problems produced agreement above chance level; since the test treats executions as independent, these deviations should be read as descriptive rather than inferential. Top-3 Accuracy ranges from 10.1% to 72.1% across problems, relative to chance baselines of 30% to 75%. Reliability varies strongly across problems, and the compensatory/non-compensatory distinction from the pilot does not fully explain this. In this pipeline, the scoring stage receives the names of the alternatives and criteria but not the numerical decision data, so the results reflect the LLM’s prior knowledge; its role as an explanatory factor is proposed as a hypothesis for future testing.

Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them. Overall, TRUST has revealed 46 faults across six popular SAST tools, 17 of which have been confirmed. In addition, our study yields ten empirical findings and four practical lessons that provide actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools.

Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs' inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to quantify psychological constructs from natural language, yet their outputs are typically evaluated only as predictions of an external label. When that label is itself imperfect, optimizing prediction conflates label agreement with construct measurement. No study has applied a multidomain measurement-oriented evaluation to LLM-derived psychological outputs. Objective We applied 5 psychometric evaluation domains to LLM-derived outputs to test whether measurement-oriented evaluation surfaces properties that prediction-oriented evaluation does not: extraction repeatability, convergent validity with a lexicon-based tool, ecological concurrent validity decomposed into within-person and between-person components, incremental value in a 4-arm comparison with that tool, and method-blinded expert evaluation with structured error attribution. Methods Thirteen linguistic features were extracted by GPT-5.2 (OpenAI) from 3556 person-days of daily voice narratives collected from 279 call center workers over 15 days via ecological momentary assessment. Features were evaluated across the 5 domains, with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count, version 22, as the lexicon-based comparator. Multimodel robustness was assessed by re-extracting all features with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash. Results Features showed high repeatability (mean intraclass correlation coefficient=0.987), construct-dependent convergent validity (Spearman ρ=0.08 to 0.79), and within-person tracking of same-day stress (negative emotion β=0.68). In a 4-arm comparison (baseline, baseline plus lexicon features, baseline plus LLM-derived features, and baseline plus both), LLM features increased explained variance in daily stress from 13.2% to 30.4%, versus 16.9% for the lexicon-based comparator. Among transcripts sampled for maximal method discordance, experts preferred LLM-derived profiles in 83.7% (261/312) of blinded decisions. Error analysis showed that 53% (35/66) of false-positive attributions reflected reference-label limitations, not model failures. Re-extraction with Google Gemini 2.5 Flash replicated key properties (person-level r =0.94). Three phenomena were visible under measurement-oriented evaluation that prediction-oriented evaluation does not typically examine: divergence between within-person and between-person effects, reference-label limitations as a dominant error source, and moderation of feature meaning by individual differences. Conclusions Prediction metrics alone are insufficient for evaluating LLM-derived psychological measures. Measurement-oriented evaluation revealed properties, including level-dependent effects and asymmetric error attribution, that have direct implications for how LLM-based assessment studies interpret their results. For clinical use, the measure is a complement to existing screening instruments for longitudinal monitoring, not a stand-alone diagnostic.

This study evaluated intrinsic and extrinsic motivation determinants affecting faculty job performance and retention at Asian Institute of Computer Studies (AICS) Commonwealth, Quezon City (N=35). Using descriptive-correlational design, findings revealed very high intrinsic motivation (M=4.51 fulfillment, M=4.40 autonomy) but low extrinsic salary satisfaction (M=2.68). Regional salary disparities were identified as major push factor (M=4.11) prompting migration to public institutions, with uncertain 3-5 year retention (M=3.06). Five policy interventions are proposed: compensation restructuring, workload optimization, non-monetary pathways, facilities upgrade, and participative leadership.

Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence chatbots, particularly ChatGPT, have emerged as increasingly popular sources of health information for the general public. However, concerns persist regarding the accuracy, safety, and appropriateness of AI-generated medical advice, especially for life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction. Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, completeness, and safety of ChatGPT-generated responses and information to public questions about heart attacks, assess user perceptions and trust, and compare AI-generated content with expert-validated sources. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between January and March 2026. A total of 73 commonly asked heart attack-related questions were submitted to ChatGPT (GPT-4), and responses were independently evaluated by two expert reviewers and one external reviewer using standardized rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, clarity, safety, and tone. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients. In parallel, a survey of 352 participants evaluated user perceptions, trust, and behavioral use of ChatGPT for medical information. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlation analyses, and multivariable regression models to identify predictors of trust and satisfaction. Results: Expert reviewers assigned high ratings for accuracy (mean: 4.62 ± 0.62 and 4.48 ± 0.63) and safety (mean: 4.78 ± 0.51 and 4.05 ± 0.50), with substantial inter-rater agreement (ICC = 0.788). In contrast, the external reviewer documented considerably lower completeness ratings (2.59 ± 0.57), revealing deficiencies in information coverage. Remarkably, 40.6% of respondents indicated they had followed ChatGPT's medical recommendations without seeking professional consultation, while 17.6% reported depending on the chatbot during urgent medical situations. Levels of user trust and satisfaction were moderate, showing significant correlations with perceived accuracy, usage frequency, and healthcare-related educational background. Conclusions: Expert assessments confirmed that ChatGPT generally provides accurate and safe cardiovascular health information; nevertheless, considerable inter-reviewer variability—especially the markedly lower completeness scores from the external evaluator—reveals significant gaps in content depth. These results indicate that ChatGPT functions more appropriately as an adjunctive educational resource rather than a replacement for professional medical consultation, emphasizing the necessity for enhanced safety mechanisms, clearer user instructions, and standardized content protocols when addressing high-stakes health topics. ChatGPT should be considered an adjunctive resource rather than a substitute for urgent professional medical assessment in suspected heart attack cases.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Computational chemistry has become a strategic component of drug design by enabling the evaluation of large chemical libraries, the investigation of molecular interactions, and the prioritization of candidates before experimental testing. This mini-review examines the evolution of computational chemistry applied to virtual screening, highlighting its main approaches, the physicochemical filters used for compound selection, and the incorporation of artificial intelligence-based methods. A narrative review of the literature was conducted using Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, SciELO, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by Google Scholar. Publications from 2015 to 2026 were prioritized, along with seminal studies on the Lipinski, Ghose, Egan, Muegge, and Veber filters. The literature indicates that structure-based and ligand-based drug design provide complementary strategies for the identification and optimization of bioactive molecules. Methods such as molecular docking, molecular dynamics, QSAR, pharmacophore modeling, and ADMET prediction improve selection efficiency, whereas descriptors such as molecular weight, lipophilicity, solubility, polar surface area, ionization, flexibility, and the fraction of sp³ carbons (Fsp³) aid in assessing pharmacokinetic potential. Machine learning and deep learning have expanded the ability to explore vast chemical spaces and predict molecular properties. However, the reliability of computational results depends on the quality of the structures, data, and models employed. In conclusion, integrating computational tools, physicochemical criteria, and experimental validation can reduce costs, support decision-making, and increase the efficiency of therapeutic candidate discovery.
topics: Synthesis and Characterization of Heterocyclic Compounds

documents.abstract: This qualitative study examined K-2 early childhood educators' perceptions of Project Read AI, an artificial intelligence platform designed specifically to support phonics-based instruction aligned with the Science of Reading. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, the study investigated both the perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of the platform among six kindergarten through second-grade teachers at a suburban New York elementary school. Findings indicated that educators perceived the platform as generally user-friendly and expressed strong intentions to integrate it into their practice. Evaluations of instructional materials yielded mixed results: the Decodable Game was viewed as a highly effective engagement tool, the Lola Science of Reading chatbot produced lesson frameworks valued as supplemental resources, and the Decodable Text Generator showed instructional promise but required improvements. Implications are given for educator practice, professional development, and future research on AI-powered literacy tools in early childhood education.

Cities are central to the climate challenge, but much research on urban climate action still focuses on emissions reductions within existing systems. This literature review assesses existing research and literature, including work on human-need-driven innovation for global sustainability and the export of globally sustainable solutions. Rather than limiting urban climate action to measures aimed at reaching zero emissions, the review examines an expanded urban innovation agenda in which cities are studied as incubators and exporters of innovations that support flourishing lives for all on a flourishing planet. The review synthesizes insights from sustainability transitions, sociotechnical systems, well-being economics, artificial intelligence, and brain science. Case studies from different cities illustrate how some urban innovation agendas are already shifting. The comparison highlights how a focus on flourishing lives can mobilize start-ups, youth, and public institutions, while addressing equity and positioning cities as actors in the next generation of urban climate action.

Aim of the study. To evaluate the effect of feed bowl design on the eating behavior of domestic cats with emphasis on the phenomenon of whisker stress. Materials and methods. A prospective within-subject study with sequential exposure to two feeding conditions was conducted in 26 clinically healthy domestic cats. Animals were sequentially fed from a standard deep narrow bowl (control) and a wide shallow bowl (experiment) with a 3-day adaptation period. The following parameters were recorded: amount of feed consumed, amount of dropped feed, number of approaches to the bowl, presence of pauses and attempts to extract feed with a paw. Statistical analysis was performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Fisher's exact test and binomial test. Results. No statistically significant differences in feed consumption were found between the two conditions (p > 0,05). When using the wide shallow bowl, no feed dropping was observed (0%), whereas when feeding from the standard bowl, dropping occurred in 38,5% of cats (p < 0,05). In the preference test, cats did not show a preference for either bowl (p > 0,05). Behavioral markers of sensory discomfort were not recorded. Conclusions. Bowl design affects feeding ergonomics and the amount of spilled feed but does not confirm the existence of whisker stress as a systemic phenomenon in domestic cats. Recommendations for the use of wide bowls may be justified by practical considerations of convenience.

Fast-track total knee arthroplasty (TKA) asks patients to understand early mobilization, early discharge, opioid-sparing analgesia, and selective use of drains and catheters. We evaluated expert-rated quality of ChatGPT responses to patient questions about these pathway-specific concepts alongside conventional TKA questions. In this cross-sectional evaluation, three arthroplasty surgeons independently scored responses to 50 conventional TKA and 20 investigator-developed fast-track questions in four domains on 5-point scales. The conventional questions were selected by a multidisciplinary panel; the fast-track questions did not undergo the same selection process. Response-level means were compared descriptively and with exploratory Mann-Whitney U tests. Seventy responses received 210 expert assessments. Recalculated mean ± SD scores across individual ratings were 4.99 ± 0.15 for accuracy, 4.98 ± 0.14 for completeness, 4.98 ± 0.17 for safety, and 5.00 ± 0.07 for readability. Each of the 20 fast-track responses received a score of 5 from each of the three raters in all four domains (Supplementary Table S1). Nevertheless, question-set construction differed and scores clustered at the ceiling, so the exploratory comparison does not establish equivalence. Experts gave high ratings to the evaluated responses, including those on fast-track concepts. The observed data do not establish equivalence between question sets: the fast-track ratings require source-data verification, the sets were selected differently, and scores were concentrated at the maximum. Clinician review remains appropriate for protocol-dependent and safety-related advice. Not applicable.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Genetic disorders affect millions worldwide, posing major challenges for accurate diagnosis and effective treatments. New developments in genomic technologies, especially Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), have enhanced the classification of genetic modification and improved diagnostic abilities. Moreover, the Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methods emerged as efficient tools for evaluating the intricate genomic data and determining the patterns, which can be generally complex to identify by employing conventional analytical techniques. Additionally, the Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has developed as a significant constituent in the analysis of genomic data by enhancing the interpretability of DL methods and showing the contribution of main genetic features involved in the detection of genetic disorders. This study presents an Explainability-Aware Heterogeneous Temporal Graph Transformer for Automated Genetic Disorder Detection (XHTGT-AGDD) approach. The primary objective of the proposed model is to improve the reliability and accuracy of genetic disorder detection from genomic data by integrating advanced techniques. Initially, preprocessing is performed using quantile transformation to normalize the input data for robust analysis. Following preprocessing, feature selection is performed using the fire hawk optimizer to identify the most informative feature subsets from the genomic data. Besides, the classification task is accomplished using a heterogeneous temporal graph transformer, which captures complex relationships and temporal dependencies among genomic features. To further refine the learning process, hippopotamus optimization algorithm is employed for model optimization. In addition, an explainability mechanism based on SHAP is incorporated to interpret the model predictions and highlight the individual genetic features toward the final decision. The experimental result analysis of the XHTGT-AGDD model is performed using a benchmark dataset. The simulation results reported the enhanced results of the XHTGT-AGDD technique in terms of several measures, achieving an accuracy of 99.12%. Therefore, the proposed model provides reliable and effective performance for automated genetic disorder detection from genomic data.

This chapter reviews the development of video summarisation using handcrafted features and deep learning models, the recent advances in transformer-based, vision-language, multimodal learning, and large language models for video summarisation. It introduces the main steps of the summarization pipeline: keyframes extraction, keyshots generation, importance score prediction and summary generation. Particular focus is given to explainability techniques like LIME, Grad-CAM, attention maps and multi-granular explanations, and how frame, shot, semantic, and story-level explanations can help to increase the transparency and user trust. Applications in film and media production, OTT platforms, news, education and surveillance are also discussed as well as challenges concerning explainability evaluation, computational complexity, privacy, ethics and scalability. The future involves explainable LLMs, personalized summarization, human in the loop AI, interactive systems and foundation models.

Facial paralysis is a severely disabling disorder that causes weakness or damage to facial muscles, thus leading to abnormal or asymmetric facial movements. Timely and precise detection and grading of facial paralysis is more essential for appropriate treatments and rehabilitations. Conventionally, facial image analysis was a manual process relying on expert proficiency. Recently, deep learning (DL) techniques have revolutionized the field, especially in the context of facial and clinical image analyses. While DL enables automatic, accurate facial recognition, its black-box nature restricts its use in healthcare. Therefore, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is integrated to enhance transparency that provides visual evidence for medical decision-making. This study introduces an Explainable Deep Graph Attention Learning Framework for Facial Paralysis Identification (XDGAL-FPI). The proposed model is designed to automatically identify the severity of facial paralysis using facial image data. Initially, the input images are preprocessed, including face detection and alignment, color space conversion and contrast enhancement, noise reduction, normalization, and data augmentation to improve the quality and consistency of the input data. Besides, deep feature representations are extracted using an Enhanced Residual SwinV2 Transformer. The extracted features are then provided to a Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network that models the relational dependencies between multiple facial regions, such as the eyes, eyebrows, and mouth, for precise severity classification. Additionally, to improve the training efficiency and convergence behavior of the model, the Ranger optimizer is employed. Furthermore, the GradCAM + + technique is integrated to improve model interpretability by highlighting the important facial regions that contribute to the model’s prediction. The effectiveness of the proposed model is assessed using YouTube Facial Paralysis (YFP) Updated Dataset, which contains 14, 389 images categorized into four severity levels across different facial regions. The experimental results indicate that the proposed XDGAL-FPI model achieves improved performance compared with existing approaches across various evaluation metrics. Thus, the proposed XDGAL-FPI model can serve as a reliable and interpretable tool for automated facial paralysis severity assessment. The source code of this study is available at https://github.com/researcher010-debug/XDGAL-FPI .
topics: Facial Nerve Paralysis Treatment and Research

documents.abstract: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.

Higher education institutions have been grappling with the impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) on teaching and learning. LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek, can produce high-quality text with a single prompt. This is particularly concerning in research modules, where students are expected to showcase their work in a text-based format. In this study, ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek were prompted to develop three research assessments that an LLM should not be able to complete and were subsequently prompted with the instructions generated. The purpose was to explore the influence of assessment instructions and characteristics on the ability of these models to generate complete responses. The instructions and characteristics included written text, oral discussions, physical attendance, contextual access, realistic content, lecturer approval, and the inclusion of multiple components. The most influential characteristic was the inclusion of an oral component. Other noteworthy characteristics were requiring students to attend live events and including multiple staged components. These findings contribute to the ongoing exploration of assessment design in the age of AI and LLMs.

Small, Medium and Micro Enterprises (SMMEs) play a critical role in South Africa's automotive industry by promoting economic growth, supplier development, and employment creation. However, persistent empowerment challenges continue to constrain their participation in automotive value chains and limit their contribution to youth skills development and workforce development pathways. This study aimed to explore the empowerment challenges facing SMMEs within the Nelson Mandela Bay automotive industry and to examine how these challenges influence opportunities for youth skills formation and sustainable workforce development. A qualitative case study design was adopted, employing purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 15 participants comprising SMME owners, Sector Development representatives, and Automotive Industry Development Centre (AIDC) officials. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed using six-phase thematic analysis. The findings identified six interrelated themes that constrain SMME empowerment: access and resources, skills and training, communication and information, policy and leadership, infrastructure and operations, and motivation and organisational culture. Collectively, these barriers restrict SMMEs' competitiveness, reduce their ability to participate in supplier development initiatives, and weaken their capacity to provide workplace learning opportunities, apprenticeships, and technical skills development for young people entering the automotive industry. The study concludes that strengthening institutional support, improving communication between stakeholders, expanding access to finance and infrastructure, and aligning empowerment initiatives with industry needs are essential to enhancing SMME sustainability and supporting inclusive workforce development. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on SMME empowerment by demonstrating the close relationship between enterprise development, youth employability, and regional workforce development within South Africa's automotive industry.

The logistics sector operates as a complex sociotechnical system in which digital transformation and environmental sustainability interact as interdependent subsystems. Logistics 4.0 technologies are credited with improving operational efficiency, yet how they translate into performance remains underexplored within an integrated systems framework. Drawing on a systems science perspective, this study examines how Logistics 4.0 affects logistics performance directly and indirectly through green logistics and green innovation. Survey data from 338 manufacturing firms were analysed using structural equation modelling and mediation analysis. All seven hypothesised relationships were supported: Logistics 4.0 predicted green logistics (β = 0.735), green innovation (β = 0.631) and performance (β = 0.532), and both mediators predicted performance (β = 0.647 and 0.419). The mediating channels differ in magnitude: green logistics carries a strong indirect effect (k2 = 0.331) and green innovation a moderate one (k2 = 0.203), indicating that the operational and strategic routes to sustainable performance mature on different horizons. The study contributes by modelling these constructs as complementary subsystems rather than isolated variables, and by differentiating empirically the strength of the two mediating channels. For managers and policymakers, the implication is direct: digitalisation delivers its full return only when planned jointly with sustainability capability.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday epistemic practices, yet their epistemological status remains unclear. Existing debates typically oscillate between treating LLMs as epistemic agents or reducing them to mere tools. This paper argues that both views mischaracterize the core issue. Drawing on a teleological interpretation of 4E cognition and the paradigm of human–AI coevolution, it develops an alternative account that understands LLMs as components of extended epistemic capacities, most centrally the human capacity for judgment. On this view, epistemic capacities are not intrinsic properties of isolated subjects or systems, but purposive and relational achievements enacted within sociotechnical practices. LLMs do not possess epistemic agency or original normativity; rather, they reshape the conditions under which human judgment, inquiry, understanding, and justification unfold. By analyzing language, coevolutionary feedback loops, derived normativity, and epistemic autonomy, the paper shows how epistemic responsibility remains human while epistemic performance becomes technologically extended.

Maintaining cognitive load that is neither too high nor too low is key for workplace safety and efficiency. Cognitive load assessment research is often conducted in highly controlled laboratory environments that, by nature, come short of fully recreating the everyday manufacturing floors. In this feasibility study we explore the viability of adopting eye-tracker for assessing workers’ cognitive load as they complete seatbelt manufacturing assemblies in a factory workplace. Following the industrial partner’s availability, four assembly workers were selected for this feasibility study. They wore a portable Pupil Labs eye-tracker while completing seatbelt assembly tasks. Mental task demand was measured using subjective ratings. Results showed that the quality of the eye-tracking data was high in spite of the highly dynamic full-body motions required to complete assemblies. Also, no evidence was found that the presence of the eye-tracker interfered with task completion. Tasks deemed more mentally demanding were associated with greater pupil size and blink rate, a pattern consistent with laboratory research. Despite this study’s limitations, including its small sample size, these findings represent preliminary evidence for the adoption of eye-tracking metrics for conducting cognitive ergonomics assessments on factory floors.

Abstract—Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Foundation Models on private, decentralized domain data is essential for specialized healthcare, legal, and financial enterprise applications. However, centralizing domain-specific text corpora triggers catastrophic data privacy violations under stringent regulatory mandates (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), while full-parameter federated fine-tuning incurs insurmountable communication bottlenecks (>140 GB per communication round for a 70B parameter model) and exhausts edge GPU memory. The confluence of Federated Learning (FL) and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)—designated as Fed-LLMs—establishes a scalable paradigm where decentralized client nodes collaboratively adapt foundation backbones while sharing exclusively low-rank parameter updates. Nevertheless, deploying Fed-LLMs across heterogeneous edge infrastructures introduces severe systems challenges: non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) catastrophic forgetting, communication bandwidth saturation over constrained wide-area networks, split learning intermediate activation leakage, and susceptibility to gradient inversion attacks in autoregressive attention layers. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical architectural evaluation of Federated Fine-Tuning for Foundation Models. We formalize federated low-rank adaptation (Fed-LoRA) aggregation under statistical distribution skew, derive the mathematical dynamics of Split Federated Learning (SplitFed) across partitioned transformer layers, and establish formal differential privacy bounds under DP-FedAvg. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-node testbed comprising 64 distributed client nodes fine-tuning open foundation models (Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, and Mistral-7B) across multi-tenant clinical records, financial reports, and legal jurisprudence. Our empirical findings demonstrate that quantized federated low-rank adaptation (Fed-QLoRA, rank r=8, 4-bit NormalFloat) reduces uplink communication payloads by 99.4% (from 14.2 GB down to 84 MB per round) while retaining 96.8% downstream domain accuracy compared to centralized full-parameter fine-tuning. Concurrently, activation obfuscation in SplitFed bounds reconstruction attacks to below 0.002 PSNR. Finally, we formulate open research directions in heterogeneous client rank adaptation, post-quantum secure aggregation, and federated alignment via decentralized direct preference optimization.

Large language model agents can improve their capabilities by evolving reusable natural-language skills from execution experience. In real-world deployments, this experience is distributed across data owners who cannot pool their raw data, which motivates federated skill evolution. The natural first design lets each client evolve the whole skill document and upload the result for server-side aggregation. That design is poorly matched to skill evolution for three reasons. An evolved document can still carry client-specific content distilled from private traces, repeated transmission of a nearly unchanged document spends communication on knowledge that the population already holds and the contribution of a single client is buried in a document that the server cannot meaningfully attribute. We propose FedSkillGit, a federated skill evolution framework that replaces full-document updates with commits. Each participating client submits a bounded set of patches over named rules together with its local experience, which summarizes what the round taught it, and the pair passes a two-stage privacy filter before it leaves the client. The server deduplicates the submitted patches and the local experience of all participants, updates a global experience document that only the optimizers read, and merges the surviving patches into a candidate skill. The candidate is distributed to the clients, which score it on their own validation sets and report the results, and it is published only when the reported scores improve on the current version. Experiments on three datasets and three language model families show that FedSkillGit outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 22% and approaches centralized evolution without sharing raw client data.

ABSTRACT The integration of Internet of Things (IoT) with cloud platforms has generated an extremely decentralized, data‐driven network that is transforming industries. At the same time, the integration poses intricate cybersecurity challenges because of scalability requirements, device heterogeneity, and an evolving threat environment. Conventional security metrics are inadequate in some circumstances, creating a necessity for adaptive, intelligent, and proactive defense modules. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers beneficial capabilities for intrusion detection, predictive threat modeling, anomaly detection, and malware analysis. Moreover, deep learning (DL) models have proved exceptional effectiveness in automatically learning intricate patterns from larger‐scale network traffic information, allowing precise identification of advanced cyberattacks in IoT‐cloud systems. Therefore, this manuscript presents a Fine‐Grained Hybrid Attention‐Aware Deep Learning Framework for Multi‐Layer Cyberattack Detection (FGHADL‐MLCD). The major intention of the proposed model is to enhance the reliability and intelligence of cyberattack detection in large‐scale IoT‐cloud infrastructures. The FGHADL‐MLCD approach operates through a sequence of stages, including preprocessing, attribute selection, cyberattack classification, and model optimization. Initially, the collected network traffic data from TON‐IoT and Edge‐IIoT datasets undergo preprocessing operations such as data cleaning, label encoding, feature scaling, and dataset splitting to ensure consistency of input data. Following that, an effective attribute selection mechanism is introduced using the Boruta feature selection technique, which identifies the most relevant network traffic features. For multi‐layer cyberattack detection and classification, the proposed model employs a bidirectional temporal convolutional network integrated with an attention mechanism. Furthermore, the training process of the deep learning model is optimized using the Adam optimizer. To assess the model's effectiveness, extensive experiments are conducted using the benchmark IoT cybersecurity datasets. The experimental results indicate that the proposed technique achieves improved cyberattack detection performance compared to recent models. Thus, the proposed model delivers a reliable solution for securing IoT‐cloud infrastructures against diverse and evolving cyber threats.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: Musculoskeletal injuries are a major occupational health concern in the fire service and can affect firefighter health, operational readiness, staffing, and injury-related costs. Although prior research has described the epidemiology of firefighter injuries, less is known about how firefighters perceive the causes of musculoskeletal injuries. This study examined perceived contributors to musculoskeletal injury among 113 career firefighters from two Mid-Atlantic fire departments. Firefighters completed an open-ended survey question asking them to identify the top three reasons firefighters are injured on the job. Responses were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis, and theme frequencies were summarized overall and compared across department, sex, age group, and years of service. Nine themes were identified. Insufficient physical fitness was the most frequently reported perceived contributor (75.2% of participants), followed by complacency or protocol non-compliance, fatigue and impaired sleep, improper movement technique, and limited mobility or flexibility. Perceived contributors were generally consistent across demographic and occupational subgroups. These findings suggest that firefighters perceive musculoskeletal injuries as largely related to modifiable individual and behavioral factors. Identifying firefighter-perceived causes of injury may help inform worksite prevention efforts, including fitness development, fatigue mitigation, movement education, mobility training, and reinforcement of safe work practices.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Modernizing mature scientific software from Fortran to Python can improve accessibility and integration with modern computing tools, but manual rewriting is expensive. Large language models (LLMs) make translation more practical, yet generated code can pass regression tests while violating source-language semantics, and contextual corrections may not persist across subsequent translations. We present ForTress, which solidifies recurring LLM translation decisions into guarded executable rules for deterministic reuse and provides semantic assurance for a non-trivial subset of these rules. Its LLM-assisted auditing process expresses universally quantified preservation obligations over mechanized Fortran and Python semantics in Lean. Human experts review semantic fidelity and correspondence with production rules, and Lean's kernel checks proofs and refutations under explicit assumptions. These audit records expose the conditions either supporting correctness or identifying failure cases. We evaluate ForTress on 17 benchmarks from 15 scientific software spanning diverse domains. The translated programs achieve bitwise-identical with native Fortran on all evaluated tests under the recorded execution and initialization configurations. Against these software, ForTress accumulates 193 executable rules and 188 audit records, of which 121 have checked soundness proofs, including 31 established after counterexample-guided refinement. Cross-software reuse exceeds 90% for 14 of the 15 software. Even with additional assurance and determinism, the LLM usage cost is 44.2% lower than direct LLM translation.

The valorization of agro-food by-products represents a potential strategy to address both environmental sustainability and the growing demand for innovative health-promoting products. Traditionally considered waste materials, agro-food residues are now recognized as valuable sources of bioactive compounds, including polyphenols, flavonoids, carotenoids, terpenoids, peptides, and other phytochemicals with potential nutraceutical applications. This review aims to provide a critical synthesis of the transition from agro-food by-product recovery to the development of evidence-based precision nutraceuticals. Particular attention is given to the chemical diversity of bioactive compounds obtained from representative agro-food sources, including citrus, olive, grape, tomato, and pomegranate residues, highlighting their biological activities and therapeutic potential. The molecular mechanisms underlying their health-promoting effects are discussed, focusing on key pathways involved in oxidative stress (Nrf2), inflammation (NF-κB), metabolic regulation (AMPK/SIRT1), mitochondrial homeostasis, autophagy/mitophagy, and apoptosis. Beyond the description of biological activities, this review critically addresses the main challenges limiting the translation of agro-food-derived bioactives into effective nutraceutical products, including bioavailability, bioaccessibility, intestinal metabolism, standardization of extracts, variability of raw materials, dose optimization, and the gap between preclinical findings and clinical evidence. The translational bottleneck is examined in detail, emphasizing the need for robust clinical validation and regulatory compliance. Finally, future perspectives are discussed, highlighting the potential of emerging technologies, including precision extraction, omics approaches, artificial intelligence, and personalized nutrition, to overcome current limitations and to enable the development of sustainable, safe, and effective nutraceutical interventions. By integrating advances in food science, molecular pharmacology, and human health research, this review provides a comprehensive perspective on how agro-food by-products can be transformed into scientifically validated nutraceutical platforms, supporting the development of sustainable and personalized strategies for disease prevention and health promotion. Despite promising preclinical evidence, clinical validation remains limited: most human studies are small, of short duration, and none have evaluated hard clinical endpoints.

This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence in transforming market analysis and investment strategy through machine learning-based stock direction forecasting. It proposes a standardized and reproducible evaluation framework that integrates predictive modeling, cross-firm robustness assessment, and risk-adjusted economic evaluation within a unified methodology. Using five large-cap technology firms as an empirical illustration, the chapter demonstrates how machine learning-generated market signals can support investment decisions and be evaluated using predictive accuracy, cumulative returns, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown. The findings indicate that ensemble learning methods, particularly XGBoost, provide more robust predictive signals and superior risk-adjusted performance across multiple firms. The chapter emphasizes methodological rigor, economic validation, and cross-firm consistency, providing a practical framework for AI-driven financial forecasting and investment decision support.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support self-regulated learning (SRL), but its pedagogical value depends on whether interaction elicits learner cognition or substitutes for it. This study examined how students’ reported use of GenAI corresponded to an intended question-first coaching design, the perceived processes and tensions associated with SRL, and conditions relevant to potential scale. A qualitatively driven embedded case study utilized 31 reflective portfolios as the primary dataset, complemented by 53 survey responses and 68 weekly logs from 12 maximum-variation cases. Abductive, reflexive thematic analysis generated five themes. Question-led interaction appeared most useful when it prompted problem reframing, led to a bounded evidence-producing action, and preserved learner judgment through evaluation, modification, or rejection of AI suggestions. Benefits were qualified by role drift, generic interaction, cognitive substitution, uneven engagement, and continued need for human support. The findings support a distributed coaching-system interpretation in which AI-supported elicitation, pedagogical scaffolding, learner agency, reported AI-role configuration, and function-specific human support interact. The study does not demonstrate institutional scalability; instead, it identifies scale-relevant conditions including sustained engagement, manageable scaffolding, role boundaries, safety, learner judgment, and routes to human expertise.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence has unsettled more than the labour market. It has given rise to two related anxieties: an existential unease about human meaning, agency, and uniqueness—“AI anxiety”—and a quieter abdication of critical effort to machines, which recent works call “cognitive surrender.” The remedies most often proposed for these conditions, among them psychoeducation, regulation, engineering ethics, and therapy, leave a conspicuous gap, since none of them draws on aesthetic experience or on the making of meaning. This article, written from an engaged, applied art-history position, proceeds as a conceptual analysis rather than an empirical study. It defines “mindful art engagement” as a receptive, two-phase practice that moves from bare to informed looking, an open and contemplative looking followed by art-historically informed interpretation, sets out its boundaries, distinguishes the three constructs on which it bears (felt meaningfulness, art-historical understanding, and cognitive enrichment), and maps the existing evidence onto its components. On this basis, it advances a hypothesis that such a practice could contribute to emotion regulation and to cognitive enrichment in the age of AI, and that meaning is the point at which the two pathways meet.

Throughout history, humans have continuously developed and experienced advanced technologies designed to automate labor-intensive processes and streamline herculean tasks. Currently, our generation is actively harnessing the multi-faceted power of Web 3.0 technologies, which are characterized by their comprehensive, all-around attributes. Key innovations such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality, extended reality, blockchain, non-fungible tokens, smart contracts, decentralized platforms, and intelligent learning management systems represent the vanguard of these uprising Web 3.0 tools and platforms. While these technological advancements profoundly elevate major industries including business, finance, medicine, and agriculture, they also critically upgrade our academic field. Web 3.0 tools do more than just elevate the standard teaching and learning experiences; they actively organize and manage entire college and university academic ecosystems, providing the most seamless operational experience available. By deploying these tools, college administrations can effortlessly handle multiple complex tasks simultaneously, consistently resulting in perfect project completion and execution. This paper outlines the strategic utilization of Web 3.0 tools and platforms within the respective sectors of colleges and universities to demonstrate a measurable betterment of workflow within institutional management. From immersive virtual classrooms to decentralized campus management systems, Web 3.0 tools play a vital role in redefining the professional responsibilities of academic staff, professors, students, research assistants, lab instructors, librarians, and administrative assistants. Furthermore, this paper exhibits the implementation of Web 3.0 technologies across other crucial academic dimensions, specifically highlighting research development, secure student data management, and peer-to-peer (P2P) collaboration.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) have expanded the role of conversational agents in hospitality and travel service encounters. However, it remains unclear how the conversational characteristics of AI become psychologically meaningful and relate to travelers’ sustainable decision-making. Drawing on Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT), this study examines the associations between Chatbot Conversational Quality (CCQ) and Green Travel Intention (GTI) through the sequential roles of Perceived Chatbot Empathy (PCE) and Green Travel Motivation (GTM), while considering Eco-Friendly Customer Innovativeness (EFCI) as a boundary condition. Survey data from 400 travelers show that CCQ is associated with PCE, which in turn is associated with stronger GTM and, subsequently, higher GTI. EFCI strengthens the PCE-GTM relationship but does not significantly moderate GTM-GTI, suggesting greater relevance during motivation formation than motivation-to-intention translation. The findings show how conversational AI interactions can acquire socio-emotional meaning in hospitality contexts and highlight customer heterogeneity in sustainability-related decisions.

Counterfeit goods create economic, security, and sustainability risks for supply chains, yet blockchain, radio-frequency identification (RFID), and artificial intelligence (AI) have mostly been studied as separate technologies. This study conceptualises their joint adoption as Logistics Anti-Counterfeiting Digital Technology (LACD) adoption, a converged capability combining identification, traceability, and analytical detection. Drawing on Rational Choice Theory and Deterrence Theory within a perspective informed by the Technology-Organisation-Environment framework, it examines the antecedents and outcomes of LACD adoption and the moderating role of government regulation. Survey data from 232 medium and large third-party logistics (3PL) firms in China were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling.
