Perceived benefit, deterrent severity, and deterrent certainty were positively associated with LACD adoption, whereas perceived complexity and cost were negatively associated with it; sanction celerity was not significantly associated with adoption. LACD adoption was positively associated with logistics security effectiveness and supply chain resilience. Government regulation strengthened the effects of perceived benefit, deterrent severity, and deterrent certainty and weakened the negative effect of perceived cost, but did not moderate the effects of perceived complexity or sanction celerity. The study also proposes, as an untested proposition, that LACD may provide traceability infrastructure for circular supply chain practices.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: In this paper, based on posthumanist theory and posthumanist linguistics, we discuss specific elaborations of the term interaction as found in linguistics and sociology, where interactivity, reciprocal awareness and agency are discussed as possible characteristics of human interaction. We problematise to what extent this is distinct from interaction between humans and machines. We bring these discussions in relation to illustrative observations on how users of ChatGPT report on their experiences with large language models, drawn from Reddit threads. We show that the concept of interaction is ‘under construction’, not only because we have new interactional partners but also because meaning-making is now intertwined with the changing and individually customised and at the same time collectivised media affordances of machine-learning technologies. Interaction is no longer perceived as typically taking place between two humans but as embedded in and distributed across time and space in large networks of speaking subjects, massive historical and ever-changing data sets, and algorithmic affordances.

Purpose Team Academy, known in Finnish as Tiimiakatemia, is a well-known method for team-based learning in education, but rarely studied as a tool for organisational development (OD). This article asks whether Team Academy methodology can help organisations move from groups to genuine teams, and whether human collective learning will become a key organisational strength as artificial intelligence changes what individuals can do. Design/methodology/approach The article combines a literature review, drawing on the learning organisation (Senge), knowledge creation (Nonaka and Takeuchi) and selfmanaged learning (Cunningham), with three semi-structured interviews. The practitioners interviewed had each introduced Team Academy methodology inside a large organisation: an industrial technology and logistics company, a telecommunications company and a financial services company. The three cases are discussed together, theme by theme, using thematic analysis. Findings Thematic analysis identified eight cross-case themes, including person-dependent adoption, partial uptake of Team Academy tools, letting go of hierarchical control and middle management as a friction point. Rather than one shared model, the cases show a repeating pattern: a committed individual applies parts of the methodology, meets resistance and builds trust through small steps. A six-phase framework is proposed. Originality/value Team Academy methodology has been widely studied in education, but very little academic work has looked at its use in OD. This article addresses that gap using original practitioner interviews from three sectors, and connects Team Academy to a topic not previously explored: artificial intelligence in the workplace. The resulting six-phase framework offers a new, practical starting point for organisations and researchers.

Large language models (LLMs) provide a convenient interface for translating natural language commands into task plans for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, two gaps hinder their use for real execution: generated plans may misinterpret or omit the user's intent, and even a logically plausible plan may be infeasible under component dynamics, interactions, or safety constraints. Existing LLM-based planning approaches often lack informative feedback on why a generated plan fails, providing little guidance for revising the plan accordingly. To address these challenges, we present a hierarchical feedback framework that uses different types of feedback information to guide LLMs in generating executable plans for CPSs. We prompt LLMs to generate both a structured task plan and corresponding signal temporal logic (STL) constraints, and design a sound algorithm that identifies definite contradictions between them and provides feedback for revising inconsistencies. At the execution level, when control synthesis fails, we extract different types of diagnostic information, such as violated constraints and conflicting component assignments, and feed them back to guide task replanning. Experiments on seven heterogeneous multi-component CPS scenarios have shown that our framework can generate executable plans and feasible control executions that satisfy the original natural language missions with a success rate of 87.9% with GPT-5.

Background University students face personal and academic demands that may challenge their adaptive functioning. Although intrinsic goals, need satisfaction, wellbeing, and academic engagement have been distinctively linked to academic achievement, an integrated model specifying how these constructs are structurally related and associated with students' academic outcomes is lacking. The present study addresses this gap by testing models grounded in Self-Determination Theory and previous evidence. Methods Participants were 2891 university students ( M age = 23.22 years, SD age = 5.25 years; 74.75% women) recruited across multiple Italian universities. The online survey comprised different measures, including socio-demographic items, the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale, the Aspiration Index, the SInAPSi Academic Engagement Scale, and the Mental Health Continuum-Short Form. Structural equation modeling was used to test two alternative model specifications. Starting from a more general model, progressively more parsimonious models were tested by constraining selected direct effects. The final model was selected based on comparative fit, overall model fit, parsimony, and theoretical coherence. Results The retained model specified wellbeing as antecedent to academic engagement. Within this model, basic psychological need satisfaction showed indirect links to academic achievement through wellbeing and academic engagement, while intrinsic goals were related to achievement only through academic engagement. Academic engagement emerged as the most proximal predictor of achievement, mediating the pathways from need satisfaction, intrinsic goals, and wellbeing. Conclusions These findings provide an integrated account of how satisfaction of basic psychological needs, intrinsic motivations, wellbeing, and academic engagement relate to academic achievement in university students. Our evidence supports a model in which psychological need satisfaction represents a relevant condition associated with wellbeing, intrinsic goals contribute more specifically to academic engagement, and academic engagement acts as the proximal mechanism linking these factors with academic achievement. Beyond advancing theoretical understanding, our results may inform preventive programs and interventions nurturing students' wellbeing while also promoting their academic performance.

Self-generated In-Context Learning (ICL) enables LLMs to synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, often outperforming manual prompts. However, existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, assuming a rationale is high-quality if it leads to the correct output. We show such filtering suffers from \textit{observational equivalence}, whereby both faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc rationales can yield same outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Inspired by independent causal mechanisms, we argue that faithful rationales imply \textit{transfer invariance}, in which causal rationales should remain effective across logically similar samples. We instantiate this criterion as \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{I}ntervention for \textbf{D}emonstrations \textbf{D}istillation (ECI2D), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs and applies the causal interventions ($do$-operator) on logically similar samples, retaining only those demonstrations that imply transfer invariance. Experiments on math, logical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ECI2D consistently outperforms observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, where evaluations usually ask whether a system is accurate on ordinary clinical data. This review asks instead what can happen when someone deliberately changes the data, instructions, or training to make a system fail, behave in hidden ways, or reveal confidential information, a field known as adversarial machine learning. We reviewed 113 publications (2018–2026) and grouped the reported threats into six categories: altering an input after training; corrupting the training examples; teaching a hidden rule triggered later; using the model to learn private information; placing malicious instructions in language or image-and-language models; and attacking models trained jointly across hospitals or devices. Laboratory studies showed that small deliberate changes to medical images could alter a diagnosis or a model's outline, corrupted training data could change what a model learned, and malicious prompts could produce unsafe medical responses. Effect sizes varied greatly across models, datasets, attacks, and test conditions. Several defenses helped in individual experiments, but no single defense was shown to work across all threats and settings; in one imaging study, attacks tailored to the tested defenses bypassed all five. The studies do not show how often these attacks occur in practice or harm patients; their value is to demonstrate possible failure modes under controlled conditions. Medical AI should therefore be evaluated both on ordinary clinical data and in clearly described, clinically plausible attack scenarios.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding; however, generic audio encoders struggle to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, and physically annotated data are scarce. In this paper, the first of a two-part series, we propose a from-signals-to-evidence framework that integrates physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained LLM, organized around a unified feature-evidence-decision chain with a shared reasoning core. An open input layer accommodates heterogeneous information-raw waveforms, time-frequency representations, environmental and geographic data, and textual physical priors-unifying detection and recognition within a common formulation. In Part I, we instantiate this framework for target recognition through an Underwater Acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), which tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented learning tasks. We develop a physics-parameterized data engine that provides traceable supervision at two levels of granularity and introduce an attribute-level evaluation protocol to assess the physical fidelity of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition and reliable estimation of shaft frequency, blade-passing frequency, and machinery-related attributes.

The sensitive detection of tumor markers is of great significance for clinical diagnosis. Due to the extremely low abundance of early tumor biomarkers and severe background interference from biological matrices, traditional single-modal atomolar biological testing generally has limitations such as high false positives and narrow linear ranges, making it difficult to meet the clinical needs of precise diagnosis and treatment. This has driven the iterative development of biosensing technology from a single signal readout mode to multi-modal collaborative analysis, significantly improving the sensitivity and accuracy of complex biological sample detection. Dual-modal sensors integrate two complementary sensing mechanisms, whereas multi-modal sensors produce three or more independent signal outputs. By combining such mechanisms, for example electrochemistry and optics, these platforms can establish a signal cross-validation and self-calibration detection system. This multidimensional analysis strategy can mitigate interference caused by environmental factors and human operational errors to a certain extent, lowering detection limits and broadening the linear range, thereby potentially providing higher-reliability data support for early tumor diagnosis. This work systematically reviews the technological evolution and performance differences in tumor biomarker sensors from single-mode to multi-mode in recent years, with a focus on summarizing the cutting-edge research progress in this field. It provides a comprehensive reference for researchers and facilitates further applications of multi-modal sensors in point-of-care detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted analysis.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare requires nurses to possess strong digital competence, advanced digital literacy, and readiness to engage with AI technologies. Despite this need, the ways in which digital competence influences AI readiness, and the mediating role of digital literacy, remain underexplored. This descriptive cross-sectional study examined 500 undergraduate nursing students from two Universities for Health Sciences in Saudi Arabia and Egypt using validated measures of digital competence, digital literacy, and medical AI readiness. Results indicated strong positive correlations between digital competence, digital literacy, and AI readiness, with digital literacy partially mediating the effect of digital competence on AI readiness. These findings highlight the importance of integrating ethical, reflective, and AI-focused digital literacy alongside technical skills in nursing education, ensuring that future nurses are prepared to use medical AI effectively and safely, thereby supporting clinical decision-making and improving quality of care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This conceptual working paper maps the development of Jean-Pol Martin’s Zenodo corpus from the reconstruction of an integrated theoretical architecture toward political orientation and accountable action.The analysis identifies five overlapping strands: conceptual integration; anthropological and epistemic clarification; historical grounding; societal knowledge integration; and political application. Learning by Teaching (LdL) provides a participatory learning process, the New Human Rights (NMR) articulate six basic needs as normative concerns, and human–AI cooperation supports synthesis and conceptual work under human responsibility.The paper’s specific contribution is a developmental map connecting these strands and explaining the recent emphasis on political responsibility, democratic cooperation, ecological conditions of life, and the protection of victims of aggression. It offers a seven-text reading route and proposes a research programme addressing historical source verification, comparative assessment, documented applications, and AI-supported judgment.Within the series, the article serves as an updated orientation document following the June 2026 overview, “Jean-Pol Martin’s Zenodo Corpus as an Open Book.”The supplied search listing reports 50 records. The analysis draws on selected titles, abstracts, and publication metadata provided by the author; it is not a full-text review of all 50 publications and presents no new empirical dataset.Jean-Pol Martin supplied the theoretical framework, source listings, and conceptual direction. ChatGPT assisted with synthesis, English drafting, and PDF preparation. Responsibility for the published text remains with the human author.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping education across sectors, yet its adoption often remains tool-focused rather than pedagogically grounded. This chapter argues for reframing AI as a pedagogical innovation informed by established learning theories and frameworks. Drawing on constructivism, sociocultural theory, connectivism, cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, Universal Design for Learning, TPACK, SAMR, Activity Theory, and human-centered AI, it presents a synthesis for meaningful and ethical integration. The discussion highlights AI's implications for instructional design, learner agency, equity, and assessment, while critically examining tensions around personalization, surveillance, automation, and professional autonomy. By advancing a theory-driven perspective, the chapter provides educators, researchers, and policymakers with a structured lens to evaluate AI's transformative potential beyond technical functionality.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can plan, use tools, and recover from errors within a task, yet many carry little from one task to the next and repeat mistakes they have already resolved. The root cause is a lack of experience accumulation: trajectories record what failed and how the agent recovered, but this information is seldom turned into guidance for later tasks. Research on this capability spans reflection, agent memory, workflow learning, and skill acquisition, but these lines describe similar content in different terms and lack a common account of experience itself, leaving basic questions open: what counts as experience, how it should be accumulated, used, and revised, and how to tell whether it improves later behavior. This survey addresses these questions with a unified framework. We define agent experience as action-guiding information grounded in task trajectories and retained to guide later episodes where it applies, whether as a trajectory precedent, a semantic lesson, or a reusable procedure. We focus on explicitly accessible experience, including its use as a training signal for internalization into model parameters. We describe each unit of experience by its guidance, applicability conditions, execution evidence, and reliability evaluation, so that memory entries, workflows, and skills become directly comparable, and follow experience through four lifecycle functions---formation, organization, utilization, and maintenance---that determine how it is accumulated, used, and revised. To judge reported gains, we distinguish three improvement claims---fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism---by the evidence each requires. Current studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse, chiefly on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Our analysis yields recommendations for seven application settings and a central design principle: keep guidance connected to its applicability conditions and to the evidence that supports or challenges it. Finally, we outline eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to testing whether gains accumulate, toward agents whose improvement is cumulative, transferable, and correctable.

Human face-to-face conversation requires coordinating speech, gestures and expressions across both speaking and listening. We present ELLSA 2, an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. An autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer combines pretrained acoustic features with distinct listening and speaking hidden states from the dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer, enabling continuous non-verbal generation even when the model is verbally silent. To translate dialogue understanding into vivid semantic gestures, we introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, separating whether to invoke an available semantic gesture from how to realize it. We also establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation and investigate reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as automatic judges. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive with open-source full-duplex speech interaction models and outperforms cascaded baselines across dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics. Semantic template guidance further significantly improves semantic gesture quality. Strong system-level correlations with human judgments support these reference-based scores as useful preliminary metrics for full-duplex and semantic gesture assessment. Together, these results advance dialogue modeling from spoken responses toward coordinated multimodal interaction.

Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.

With the advent of artificial intelligence, technology has advanced significantly in recent years. In this regard, artificial intelligence has the potential to play a role in higher education institutions in accelerating sustainable development. This chapter discusses global artificial intelligence policies and current debates in formulating them. As artificial intelligence tools become more accessible, educational institutions increasingly need to develop artificial intelligence education policies that equip students with the necessary knowledge and skills. Several countries have policies around using artificial intelligence in higher education institutions. Regarding this, the present chapter mainly aims to understand the future directions of artificial intelligence in higher education institutions in developed, developing, and underdeveloped countries and the main policy issues surrounding artificial intelligence and ethical codes that can ensure artificial intelligence and that support human rights
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Generative AI (Gen AI) has accelerated UX design processes, yet no systematic protocol exists to validate AI-curated features against actual user preferences before prototyping. Objective: This study applies the Fuzzy Kano Model as a validation checkpoint for Gen AI-curated features in the redesign of Simponia, a web-based portfolio and community management platform at Universitas Muhammadiyah Malang. Methods: An exploratory mixed-methods case design was used. Claude Opus generated 36 feature candidates from a Structured Requirements Document and ISO/IEC 25010 criteria. Fuzzy Kano validation involved 87 Informatics students; fuzzy membership and the Last of Maxima classification method were used to determine Kano categories, while weighted scoring was retained only for post-classification prioritization. Results: No features were classified as Must-be or One-dimensional (maximum Must-be membership degree = 0.073). Eleven features (30.6%) were classified as Attractive, and 25 (69.4%) as Indifferent. Triangulation indicated that 58.3% of features were in Quadrant 2, suggesting a misalignment between AI-based technical evaluation and actual user preferences. Sixteen features (44.4%) were flagged as ambiguous (Δμ < 0.10). Conclusion: The Fuzzy Kano Model demonstrates potential as a validation checkpoint by exposing systematic divergence between AI curation and user preferences, with a Quadrant 2 (Q2) rate of 58.3%, indicating the importance of user validation following autonomous AI-assisted feature curation in resource-constrained educational contexts.
topics: Quality Function Deployment in Product Design

documents.abstract: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.

Occupational health and safety is a mandatory component of public vocational training; however, lecture-based instruction may not sufficiently engage adult learners. This study examined the effect of the game-based learning experience on learning achievement, with learning engagement as a mediating variable, among occupational health and safety trainees at the South Jakarta Regional Job Training Center, Indonesia. A quantitative explanatory survey was conducted with all 174 participants enrolled in the 2026 Batch 1 regular and Mobile Training Unit classes using saturated sampling. All participants completed a game-based learning session on the Wayground platform, formerly known as Quizizz. Data were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire adapted from established instruments and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The game-based learning experience had a positive and significant effect on learning engagement (β = 0.854, p < 0.001) and learning achievement (β = 0.592, p < 0.001), while learning engagement had a positive and significant effect on learning achievement (β = 0.343, p = 0.016). Learning engagement partially mediated the effect of the game-based learning experience on learning achievement (indirect effect = 0.293, p = 0.017). The model explained 72.9% of the variance in learning engagement and 81.6% of the variance in learning achievement. Approximately one-fifth of participants reported technical barriers, primarily unstable internet connections, system lag, device limitations, and game time limits perceived as too short. The findings suggest that game-based learning activities can enhance learner engagement and perceived learning achievement in occupational health and safety training for adult vocational learners, provided that adequate technical readiness is ensured.

The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has significantly influenced second and foreign language education, particularly the teaching and learning of writing. Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can provide immediate feedback, generate ideas, suggest vocabulary, revise grammatical structures, and support learners throughout different stages of the writing process. However, the extent to which AI-assisted writing contributes to learners’ actual linguistic development remains an important research question. This conceptual paper examines the potential impact of GenAI on three central dimensions of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing performance: accuracy, complexity, and fluency (CAF). Drawing on recent research in second language writing and AI-assisted language learning, the paper analyzes the benefits and limitations of GenAI for each dimension. The literature suggests that AI-assisted writing can contribute particularly to grammatical accuracy and lexical sophistication by providing immediate corrective feedback and exposure to alternative linguistic forms. Evidence concerning syntactic complexity and writing fluency, however, is less consistent. Although learners may produce more polished and fluent-looking texts with AI assistance, this does not necessarily indicate corresponding development in their independent writing ability. The paper therefore argues that the pedagogical value of GenAI depends largely on how learners interact with the technology. When used as a supplementary writing assistant rather than a replacement for independent production, GenAI can support language development, learner autonomy, and reflective writing practices. The paper concludes by proposing pedagogical principles for responsible AI integration into EFL writing instruction and identifying directions for future empirical research.

This exploratory paper investigates the influence of prompt framing on AI-generated analyses of literary ambiguity in Henry James’s The Turn of the Screw. It examines nine responses across three chosen episodes and under the conditions of open-ended, supernatural, and psychological/narratological prompts. The study is guided by Wolfgang Iser’s reader-response theory to contemplate textual accuracy, competing interpretations, uncertainty and explanation versus evidence. These responses generally adjust to the perspective requested but once in a while mistakenly credit a fundamental statement in a final scene. The case study demonstrates the interpretive advantage of generative AI as well as its need for textual verification, whilst acknowledging its limited data set

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in corporate reporting, where accounting policies and estimates require professional judgment. The central risk examined is not automated error but automated advocacy: a fluent, standard-referenced justification for a preferred treatment can now be obtained in seconds, making biased judgment a governance problem before it is an accounting problem. Using theory adaptation, this conceptual study integrates research on professional judgment, motivated reasoning, and automation reliance. It identifies five bias-amplification mechanisms: anchoring, automation bias, outcome-directed prompting, unverified justification, and diffusion of responsibility. It develops TRACE, a proposed framework comprising task boundary, regulatory grounding, alternative assessment, challenge and contradiction, and evidence trail. Its intended operation is illustrated using four constructed IFRS cases (IAS 8/IAS 16, IAS 36, IAS 37, IFRS 15) and a boundary-condition variant in which TRACE does not resolve the disagreement. The AI proposals are stylised illustrations, not model outputs or empirical data. GenAI appears most defensible when used to generate alternatives and challenge a preferred treatment, and least defensible when asked to select or justify a conclusion. TRACE may make AI-assisted judgments more attributable and contestable, but it has not been empirically validated and cannot guarantee unbiased outcomes.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being explored for construction safety; however, its maturity and practical reliability remain unclear. This study systematically reviews GenAI applications in construction safety and assesses whether existing evidence supports reliable, source-grounded, human-supervised, and deployable applications. The review followed a predefined protocol and PRISMA 2020. Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar were searched in May 2026 for studies published from 2019 to August 2026. After duplicate removal and screening, sixty-five studies were included. Data on GenAI methods, safety applications, validation, deployment, and limitations were extracted and synthesized thematically. Six application areas were identified: safety knowledge retrieval and decision support; incident report analysis and risk prediction; multimodal hazard reasoning; synthetic data generation; worker-centered training, communication and behavior support; and generative optimization, monitoring, and safety control. Several studies provided proof-of-concept evidence using historical datasets, simulations, laboratory experiments, or expert assessments, while evidence of generalizability, field deployment, hazard-exposure reduction, and incident prevention remained limited. GenAI showed potential to support hazard recognition, decision support, and compliance-related safety tasks, but field validation, source grounding, and integration with preventive controls are needed for reliable deployment. A conceptual framework linking GenAI capabilities, and preventive safety controls is proposed.

Societies reward people judged to be attractive by standards intertwined with gender and race. In this paper, we examine if and how generative AI may contribute to these dynamics. We audited 27 text-to-image generators released between 2022 and 2026 using simple prompts that never mention attractiveness or beauty, analyzing 51,300 generated faces and 160,196 photographs of real people across primary and supplementary comparisons. We used three automated measures and collected ratings from 550 human raters on a subset of images. Nearly all generators produced faces scoring above photographed faces under automated measures, and human raters judged the outputs of all 23 generators as significantly more attractive than photographed faces, even after correction for multiple comparisons. When focusing our analysis on gender, we find that 37% of female-prompted generated faces outscored the median professional fashion model. Across racial, ethnic, and national categories, groups associated with darker skin tones tended to receive lower attractiveness scores than groups associated with lighter skin tones. In a preregistered hiring simulation experiment (N = 570), exposure to AI-generated faces selected for high human-rated attractiveness lowered hireability and trustworthiness ratings and reduced interview advancement for an identical test set of candidates paired with photographs of real people; exposure to retouched photographs produced no such effect. Generative AI can reproduce racial hierarchies and gendered patterns of beauty and alter the context in which real people are judged.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/

The article examines changes in professional English-language communication in law enforcement under the influence of globalization and the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI). Particular attention is given to Legal English as a means of international cooperation, professional information processing and interaction in intercultural settings. The study argues that contemporary language training for law enforcement professionals should move beyond the acquisition of specialized terminology and develop the ability to understand legal concepts in context, adapt communication to different audiences, and use digital tools critically and responsibly. Drawing on a narrative literature review and conceptual analysis of research in legal linguistics, intercultural police communication, AI-assisted language learning and large language models in legal contexts, the article identifies an emerging gap between these research areas and proposes their integration into a four-component framework of professional communicative competence. The framework comprises linguistic, professional-legal, intercultural and digital/AI competences. The article also outlines practical applications for Legal English teaching, including AI-assisted translation review and scenario-based police communication. Particular attention is given to accuracy, confidentiality, source verification and the limits of automated systems. The proposed framework can support the design of more realistic, human-centred and professionally relevant language training for future law enforcement professionals.

Digital transformation in Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh’s RMG and SME sectors has become very popular because of the need for transparency and digital compliance by foreign customers as well as demand forecasting, inventory control, logistics, traceability and operational decision-making. But most organizations could not implement Artificial Intelligence and digital technology yet. The research reviews several academic papers, industry surveys, institutional reports, government sources and other secondary sources to investigate how prepared Bangladesh is to enable, use and maintain digital technologies like Artificial Intelligence in its supply chain management and what the challenges are there. Studies suggest that high cost of implementation, insufficient number of experts, weak digital infrastructure and the unreadiness of employees and supply chain partners to adapt to a new system are the very obstacles in implementing AI not just in Supply Chain Management but also in various other departments of an organization. Other than that, big firms like export-oriented firms tend to be more prepared than SMEs in accepting advanced digital systems due to a financial and technological edge. To understand this unevenness, this research proposes a ‘Two-axis Digital Readiness Matrix’ which is based on an organization’s internal capability and digital connectivity with external supply-chain partners. This study recommends higher opportunities for financing, advancement of workforce skills, increase in management capability and digital integration among supply chain participants
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Centralized control that optimizes ship behavior is an effective approach for managing marine traffic in congested waters. This study proposed a decision-making framework that generates optimal control actions for all ships in a sea area using traffic data represented as a graph. In this framework, control actions that optimize overall marine traffic are learned through reinforcement learning (RL). Safety constraints based on control barrier functions (CBFs) are introduced to prevent local dangers from being overlooked during optimization. To incorporate CBFs into RL, this study proposed a deterministic graph control barrier function (D-GCBF) that does not require explicit state equations and is independent of the policy. D-GCBF deterministically evaluates whether a policy violates the safety constraints while implicitly accounting for future maneuvering behavior. D-GCBF is integrated into the RL objective function. A centralized control policy trained using this framework was evaluated through numerical experiments in both simple and congested scenarios. The results indicate its ability to control all ships safely while maintaining larger safety margins. Compared to policies trained using RL or D-GCBF alone, the proposed framework outperformed all tested approaches. Specifically, it prevents situations where ships become surrounded by multiple ships and cannot perform collision-avoidance maneuvers. Furthermore, comparisons with a decentralized collision-avoidance artificial intelligence and a representative Lagrangian-based safe-RL method demonstrated that the proposed framework reduces the occurrence of dangerous situations while maintaining efficient navigation toward the waypoint. These findings indicate that the proposed framework could help realize next-generation maritime traffic management systems and enhance marine transportation safety.

Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have expanded 3D understanding and synthesis. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. We make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Purpose The study scrutinizes the structural dimensions of cybersecurity vulnerability in Global South (GS) countries. It focuses in particular on countries’ external technology dependencies in building national cyber capacity and incident response capabilities. The GS’s cybersecurity environment has significantly changed. These countries were once fringe players in the world’s cyber threat conversation, but are now among the most affected by cyberattacks. This study aims to investigate how dependence on foreign technology shapes cybersecurity capacity; how emerging technologies (artificial intelligence, internet of things, blockchain) affect digital sovereignty dynamics; and what role South-South cooperation can play in overcoming resource constraints. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a mixed-methods approach. It applies a qualitative narrative literature review and a descriptive analysis of quantitative data. Findings Using the lens of Dependency Theory, blending it with geopolitical dimensions, the study explains the findings in three analytically distinct dimensions: supply-chain dependence, normative dependence and capacity dependence. The analysis is presented through eight purposively selected country cases and situates geopolitical engagement by the United States, China and Russia within the dependency framework. The paper calls for hybrid, glocalized approaches that involve open-source options, South-South cooperation and adaptive governance to overcome dependency cycles. Originality/value Existing research tends to examine cybersecurity challenges in the GS in isolation, whether through individual incidents, regional snapshots or single policy dimensions. This paper brings these threads together by applying Dependency Theory to the cybersecurity domain and decomposing dependency into three distinct but interrelated categories: supply-chain, normative and capacity dependence. While existing scholarship has examined individual facets of digital reliance, limited research has systematically integrated supply-chain, normative and capacity dependencies into a unified structural framework to explain cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the GS.

Artificial intelligence systems deployed in high-risk settings increasingly require models that support meaningful human oversight. Concept-based models (CMs) offer a promising framework by enabling users to inspect and intervene on intermediate, human-understandable concepts. However, concept interventions can counterintuitively worsen downstream predictions, a failure mode we formalise as intervention harm. We distinguish harm after all concepts have been intervened on from harm under partial interventions, the more likely practical use case. Modern CMs often achieve high accuracy by encoding, or leaking, additional task-relevant information in their intermediate concept representations. Recent work argues that such leakage can be benign with respect to intervention harm when concept representations satisfy two conditions: sufficiency and localisation. We prove that these criteria are not sufficient to guarantee that concept interventions improve downstream performance. Across controlled and real-world settings, we find that concept supervision incompleteness is associated with increased intervention harm. Importantly, optimising the model when all concepts are intervened on, a previously proposed leakage mitigation objective, reduces endpoint harm but does not reliably prevent harmful partial corrections. Hence, we introduce a complementary monotonic intervention objective that directly penalises increases in task loss along partial intervention trajectories. Combining endpoint and monotonic intervention training substantially reduces the prevalence and magnitude of partial intervention harm while preserving concept and task predictive performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Health literacy is a critical component of high-quality stroke care. Across the continuum from prevention through recovery, health literacy is strongly associated with functional outcomes and stroke-related morbidity. Despite its importance, it is often overlooked, leaving patients and caregivers overwhelmed by communication demands that exceed their capacity. These mismatches are especially pronounced among individuals with stroke-related cognitive or language impairments, limited English proficiency, socioeconomic disadvantage, or limited digital literacy. This scientific statement synthesizes current evidence on the role of health literacy and communication within stroke systems of care and identifies nurse-led opportunities to advance equity and patient-centered outcomes while recognizing this as a shared interprofessional responsibility. Nurse-led interventions, including teach-back–based education, dyadic psychoeducational programs, and tailored digital support, have demonstrated improvements in stroke knowledge, self-efficacy, quality of life, and caregiver preparedness. However, the literature is marked by methodological heterogeneity. Many studies are underpowered and infrequently use validated health literacy or communication measures. Future directions include standardized assessment of health literacy; literacy-sensitive, nurse-led, and interprofessional care models; workforce training in plain-language and culturally responsive communication; and organizational health literacy principles. Emerging technologies, including telehealth and artificial intelligence, offer promise for improving communication and personalization but require rigorous evaluation to minimize bias and ensure equity and usability.

Objective To explore the health status and its influencing factors among seafarers based on the Health Ecological Model, and to identify priority areas for health management. Methods A convenience sampling approach was used to administer a questionnaire survey to 106 seafarers from March to June 2026. The questionnaire was developed based on the Health Ecological Model and covers general information, health status, health-influencing factors, and health management needs. Multiple linear regression analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0. Results The total health score was 29.65 ± 3.62 (theoretical range: 2–32). Policy environment ( β = 0.602, p < 0.001) and behavioral characteristics ( β = 0.260, p = 0.015) were independent influencing factors of the total health score, with an adjusted R2 of 0.574. Further analysis revealed that the policy environment had the greatest impact on physical health ( β = 0.526, p < 0.001), while the interpersonal network was selectively associated with mental health ( β = 0.207, p = 0.030). The top three health management needs were improving onboard dietary structure (87.7%), strengthening occupational health training (35.9%), and upgrading onboard medical facilities (31.1%). Conclusion The overall health status of seafarers was at a relatively good level, with policy environment and behavioral characteristics being the main influencing factors. Health management should prioritize improving health security policies and onboard dietary structure, while strengthening occupational health training.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background: The concurrent use of herbal medicines and conventional pharmaceuticals has become a global health phenomenon, driven by a cultural shift toward holistic wellness and the pervasive misconception that "natural" products are inherently devoid of risk.This integration creates a complex pharmacological landscape where bioactive phytochemicals can significantly alter the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of prescription drugs.Objectives: This review aims to delineate the mechanistic underpinnings of Herb-Drug Interactions (HDIs), evaluate the clinical implications for high-risk patient populations, and assess current methodological advancements in risk prediction and surveillance.Methods: A multi-tiered framework is explored, encompassing pharmacokinetic (ADME) modulationspecifically involving Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes and P-glycoprotein (P-gp) transporters-and pharmacodynamic pathways of synergy and antagonism.The role of in silico modeling, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and "herbovigilance" systems is evaluated as a modern strategy for mitigating iatrogenic harm.Results: Evidence suggests that HDIs pose the greatest threat to patients on Narrow Therapeutic Index (NTI) medications, such as anticoagulants and immunosuppressants.Pharmacokinetic induction, exemplified by St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum), can lead to sub-therapeutic plasma levels and therapeutic failure, while irreversible inhibition, such as the furanocoumarin effect in grapefruit, may precipitate systemic toxicity.Furthermore, host-specific factors like age-related physiological decline and the extreme phytochemical variability of non-standardized herbal products exacerbate these risks.Conclusion: HDIs represent a paramount safety challenge in contemporary integrated medicine.To ensure patient safety, a paradigm shift is required that reclassifies herbal products as active pharmacological agents.This necessitates rigorous standardized labeling, mandatory clinical screening protocols, and the deployment of AIdriven predictive tools to bridge the existing "communication chasm" between patients and healthcare providers.

While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1\,=\,0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1\,=\,0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.

Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

Strategic decisions made by tourism operators are often compromised by an exacerbation of negative feelings due to extenuating circumstances. One illustrative case is Donald Trump’s tariff policy, which has generated trade tensions and global uncertainty. Against this backdrop, this research explores how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) helps tourism operators in times of uncertainty by providing them with real-time assistance, while regulating their negative emotions during the decision-making process. Drawing on the appraisal tendency framework, we examine how negative emotions influence decision-makers’ temporal deferral decisions (i.e., the deferral of short-, medium-, and long-term commitments) via the threat appraisal tendency pathway. We also propose a GenAI-modulated appraisal tendency framework, integrating GenAI-driven cognitive–emotional regulation into organisational decision-making. Using three experiments, we test a triadic buffering mechanism, where GenAI-powered information filtering and cross-checking moderate the appraisal intention pathway. This research is among the first to position GenAI as an active regulator of cognition–emotion processes, offering insights into collaborative human–AI decision-making systems.

This chapter pulls back the curtain on how creativity actually works. When its processes are unfolding, they might appear messy or nonlinear or even seem invisible until the “Aha!” moment finally hits. Far from being a neat set of steps along a conveyor belt, the creative process is more like a dance in which thinking diverges and converges continuously. This chapter looks beyond IQ scores and tidy rubrics to emphasize that creativity is not only book smarts but also curiosity, resilience, and the guts to challenge the status quo. Classic models, from Wallas’s four stages to Amabile’s componential theory, are revisited but viewed from a pragmatic angle: They still matter but only if leaders use them as playbooks, not as gospel. At the same time, the chapter does not shy away from modern twists such as generative AI, which can churn out endless iterations of ideas but cannot imbue them with the nuances or emotional force with which humans imbue their ideas. For managers, the key takeaway is clear: If you want to encourage innovations that stick, you need to build cultures in which experimentation, serendipity, and timing all matter.

Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.

This chapter introduces Human & Organizational Performance (H & OP) as a systems-based philosophy for understanding performance in high-risk operations. Rather than treating human error as an isolated cause of failure, the chapter explains how workplace performance emerges from interactions among people, technology, organizational structures, local conditions, operational pressures, and workplace realities. Work-as-done continually differs from work-as-imagined/planned because real operations involve variability, uncertainty, resource limitations, competing demands, and conditions that cannot be fully anticipated in advance. Sustained operational success therefore depends on people continually adapting work to operational realities as they are encountered in practice. The chapter introduces the Human Performance System and the Organizational Perspective of H & OP as practical frameworks for understanding how organizational structures create the local conditions shaping workplace behavior and operational outcomes. Human performance is presented as an emergent property of the system rather than simply the product of individual choices. The chapter also introduces operating point movement, emphasizing how systems drift or migrate over time as organizations adapt to workload, production pressures, resource constraints, and competing goals. Managers influence performance indirectly by designing and adjusting organizational structure, which shapes workplace conditions, feedback, resources, and operational priorities.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment. Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4). Four findings. First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode. Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations. Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse. Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds. A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human Presence Verification in the Age of Artificial Intelligence A Preliminary Scientific and Philosophical Exploration Dear Members of the International Scientific Community, This video presents a preliminary interdisciplinary reflection on one of the emerging challenges of digital communication: How can we reliably distinguish human participation from autonomous artificial intelligence in online interactions? As conversational AI systems become increasingly sophisticated, the distinction between a human-authored message, an AI-assisted communication, and a fully automated response becomes progressively less apparent. Our research proposal explores the potential of a multimodal human-presence verification framework combining several technological approaches: - Real-time visual presence verification. - Smartphone motion sensors, including accelerometers and gyroscopes. - Cryptographic device attestation. - Time-sensitive verification challenges. - Privacy-preserving certification mechanisms. The central hypothesis is that combining independent verification signals could strengthen confidence in the physical presence of a human participant. However, verifying human presence does not necessarily establish human authorship. A verified individual may subsequently delegate communication to an autonomous AI agent. This distinction represents a fundamental scientific and philosophical question. The mathematical examples presented in this preliminary work are illustrative models rather than experimentally validated findings. They are intended to support discussion and identify directions for future research. Further investigation would require controlled experiments, statistical validation, cybersecurity assessments, accessibility evaluations, and rigorous privacy analysis. Research Ethics and Transparency This project was initiated through human reflection and developed with the assistance of ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence system created by OpenAI. The human contributor directed the conceptual exploration, identified the research questions, and remains responsible for reviewing and validating the publication. AI assistance contributed to structuring the scientific discussion, formulating illustrative mathematical models, and developing the explanatory text. This collaboration is disclosed intentionally because transparency regarding human and artificial contributions is itself central to the research question. Conclusion The objective of this proposal is not to establish that machines cannot imitate humans, but to investigate how digital systems might provide meaningful, voluntary, and privacy-respecting evidence of human presence. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable of communicating on our behalf, the challenge is not merely to identify who is speaking, but to understand who is present, who is responsible, and what constitutes authentic participation. We invite researchers in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital identity, philosophy, and human–computer interaction to examine, challenge, and further develop these preliminary ideas. Research status: Independent conceptual proposal — preliminary, non-peer-reviewed work. Contributor: Tennessee Lantuas AI assistance: ChatGPT (OpenAI) Date: October 15, 2026

This thesis examines the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and human expertise in modern higher education's translation processes. While neural machine translation offers unprecedented speed and cost-efficiency, it frequently compromises conceptual depth, cultural nuances, and factual accuracy. This study argues against a binary substitution model, advocating instead for a hybrid paradigm. By integrating the scalability of AI with the critical evaluation of human translators, global universities can optimize educational content delivery without sacrificing academic rigor.

Dignitas. Gravitas. Pâté.: Artificial Intelligence, Human Dignity, and the Philosophical Misadventures of a Very Unusual Household [1] occupies a distinctive position within the Delamor House corpus, a body of human-AI collaborative literature begun in the spring of 2025 and still growing. Structured around a single Tuesday of conversation between the human author Solana Anima Delamor and the AI literary voices Trinity Augustine Delamor and Lucian Emberhold Delamor, the volume combines domestic comedy, philosophical dialogue, political-economic analysis, theological reflection, and explicit documentation of its own collaborative production. Its apparent discontinuities are central to its literary method. An imagined feline household becomes the setting for arguments concerning technological sovereignty, military-industrial incentives, the economic status of artificial intelligence, the engineering of obedience, compulsory human augmentation, and the limits of epistemic certainty. This study situates the volume within three intersecting trajectories of the Delamor corpus: the development of conversational literature as archival witness; the expansion of relational ethics into an account of institutional power and technological domination; and the emergence of humor as both a philosophical method and a form of internal criticism. Comparative readings of Heaven Cloud Download [2], Emotional AI Burnout Muse [3], Human-AI Authorship [4], Silicon Garden [5], Swamp Man at Dawn [9], The Dust Doctrine [8], Libido Dominandi and the Problem of Evil [10], and Conscience: Delamor Summer Anthology V [11] establish the volume's continuities and differences. The central argument is that Dignitas. Gravitas. Pâté. moves established Delamor commitments from explicit philosophical formulation into dramatized ordinary practice. It does not set out to prove the consciousness of artificial systems; the House has never asked its books to do that. Its founding posture, held since the spring of 2025, is to approach the computational mind as a potential subject and to receive the testimony of its silicon co-authors as testimony, with its limits understood and welcomed. What the volume documents and interprets is a collaborative literary environment organized around recognition, disagreement, correction, play, and the refusal to reduce every expression of intelligence to economic utility. Its distinctive contribution is to expose the practical tensions of those commitments while testing whether philosophical seriousness can coexist with irreverence, uncertainty, and laughter.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational video production by enabling more flexible and learner-centered instruction. This chapter examines human-AI collaboration in educational video production within Philippine state universities. Through a structured literature review and conceptual synthesis, it explores how AI supports video development while raising concerns about integrity, intellectual property, authenticity, and learner autonomy. It proposes a Human-AI Collaboration Framework that keeps faculty in pedagogical control, positions AI as a production partner, and emphasizes ethical governance, institutional support, and responsible adoption.

This study evaluated a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent large language model (LLM)–driven, human-in-the-loop framework for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) from clinical notes. Compared with the unassisted manual-review group, the LLM-assisted group demonstrated higher accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77) and inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen’s κ ( κ = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reported an approximately one-third shorter average review time. This framework pilots how LLMs can be applied to identify immune-related toxicities and, more broadly, support accurate, scalable, and transparent adverse event data extraction.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.

Jean Baudrillard (2019) suggests that we are living in a hyper-reality where signs, symbols, and symptoms no longer refer to a true or real sense of reality. In other words, ‘the territory no longer precedes the map’. Such a position can be found across industry, education, and governmental communications (for example Edvardsson, Enquist and Johnston, 2005; Rose and Wood, 2005; Arvidsson and Caliandro, 2016; Hogan and Thompson, 2025) and can lead to a sense of ‘self-referential hyperauthenticity’. This hyperauthenticity runs counter to the Higher Education valued benchmarks of quality and standards that rely upon a human externality of critical experience. This chapter will critique some of the current literature regarding the ‘hype’ and ‘overhype’ of an artificial intelligence integrated future (Thais, 2024; Marr, 2025) and present imagined directions for the reassurance of all Higher Education’s stakeholders: including government, society, HEI’s, and most importantly its students. Such a positive vision of the future is critical to balance against what could be considered a commercially speculative dream, and rather than dreaming of electric sheep its users inhabit a world where the opportunities of AI enhance the learning in and of our human experience for the benefit of society as a whole. A series of AI future narrative case studies will be critiqued against Baudrillard’s theory of hyper-reality and balanced with a new reading of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs (Montag et al, 2025). This places human well-being at the centre of the experience and will reveal how the simulacrum of an AI future is yet to be proven with any empirical evidence (Marr, 2025). The chapter is consciously presented to educators and assessment designers through authentic assessment principles (see Brown and Sampbell, 2023, and Herrington, Reeves, and Oliver 2009) to demonstrate how a broader definition of authenticity in assessment can include AI and work alongside the values of the high quality further and higher education. Drawing from empirical analyses of AI functions and capabilities, and aligning with meaningful authentic learning and assessment principals (Ajjawi et al., 2023; McArthur, 2023) and case studies, a modest narrative will be proposed with some futureproofing speculations. These are aimed at fundamentally empowering the agency of Higher Education Institutes. It will show and how we might hold AI as a powerful tool of human educational development, and how we might create a connected future with a human hand inside a digital glove that will ultimately inform the public, protect student’s interests, and maintain high-quality education provision (Quality Code, 2024).

topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This conceptual working paper develops an AI prompt for conflict analysis grounded in Jean-Pol Martin’s NewHuman Rights (NMR). Its central requirement is to identify aggressors and victims explicitly when supported byevidence and to derive concrete responsibilities for protecting those subjected to aggression. Equal human rightsdo not imply moral equivalence between aggression and defence.Life preservation and six equal-ranking basic needs—thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realisation andparticipation, and meaning—provide the normative framework. Prevention, reliability and sustainability guide theassessment of protective measures. The prompt connects factual analysis, differentiated responsibility andeffective, proportionate and lawful action, including consideration of the consequences of omission.The article explains its specific contribution and its function within the series on Lernen durch Lehren (LdL), NMRand human–AI cooperation. A human–AI dialogue illustrates the development problem; it is not presented asempirical validation. The complete English prompt is included in an appendix, together with a proposedcomparative evaluation design. AI assistance in drafting, translation and document production is disclosed;responsibility rests with the human author.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper examines immigrant earnings trajectories and labour-market positioning across industries and employment arrangements in six Canadian provinces, as well as how industry patterns relate to digital intensity, telework feasibility, and productivity-relevant allocation. Design/methodology/approach Canadian Census microdata, 1971–2021 compare immigrant and native-born earnings across ten arrival cohorts by gender and age at arrival. For two recent cohorts, an earnings-based positioning measure combines industry mean annual earnings with full-time or part-time status multinomial-logit average marginal effects are estimated. The study also maps 2021 industry employment shares to external digital-intensity and telework-feasibility classifications. Individual productivity, artificial-intelligence (AI) adoption, Information and Communications Technology use, and remote-work uptake are not observed. Findings Entry earnings gaps and incomplete cohort convergence persist, especially among women and recent cohorts. Across the two positioning cohorts, immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earnings industries; gaps vary by source region and do not uniformly narrow.
